claims.text: High-entropy-alloy protective coatings can achieve superior wear resistance through sliding-induced formation of a self-organized nanostructured oxide or glaze layer.
The wear-induced oxide or glaze layer adapts to local stresses.
The oxide or glaze layer reduces both adhesive and abrasive wear.
The as-deposited coating has a homogeneous solid-solution matrix containing dispersed intermetallic phases.
Changing alloy composition can alter oxidation kinetics.
Sliding wear produces a continuous nanostructured oxide or glaze layer on the coating surface.
Frictional heating and localized stresses accelerate oxidation during sliding wear.
Selective oxidation of alloying elements is governed by their redox potentials and atomic sizes.
The adaptive oxide layer minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact.
Coatings tested in ambient air will have lower friction coefficients and wear rates than coatings tested in inert argon.
Compositions less prone to oxidation will have higher friction coefficients and wear rates than oxidation-promoting compositions.
The mechanism should operate in high-entropy-alloy coatings containing a balance of elements that permits selective oxidation.
At sufficiently high operating temperatures, mechanical instability of the oxide layer can make the mechanism ineffective.
The mechanism will be ineffective if the alloy composition completely resists oxidation.
The optimal oxide composition and microstructure, and the quantitative threshold for effective protection, are not yet determined.
Failure to form an oxide in ambient air, or absence of a significant wear-performance difference between oxidizing and inert conditions, would falsify the hypothesis.
